text.hook:
"It's std::atomic, so it's thread-safe."
That answer stops most C++ interviews short.

Here is what atomics and CAS really guarantee, plus 6 myths. Save it. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The three-part contract of std::atomic
2. Which expressions are really one atomic step
3. CAS on failure, and the retry loop
4. Lock-free is not guaranteed
5. Atomic or mutex?
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: `std::atomic<int> a{0};` then `std::atomic<int> b = a;` Does it compile? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. std::atomic is not copyable or movable. `std::atomic<int> b = 0;` is fine since C++17 (guaranteed copy elision).

slides.lead: The contract interviewers check, and the answers that fail.

slides.title: `std::atomic<T>` promises three separate things
rows: No torn values. No lost updates on a read-modify-write (RMW).
One order of all writes to *this one object*, agreed by every thread.
What it says about *other* memory. Set by the `memory_order` argument.
slides.takeaway: Each **operation** on **one object** is indivisible. Not a sequence, not two objects.

slides.title: For `std::atomic<int> x`
rows: ✅ one atomic RMW, never loses updates
❌ atomic load, then atomic store: lost updates, no UB
❌ same gap between two atomic operations
slides.takeaway: A race condition (lost update) is a logic bug. A data race is UB. Know which one you have.

slides.title: What `compare_exchange_strong` does
bullets: `expected` is taken **by reference** and **overwritten** on failure.
Compares bits, not `operator==`: `+0.0` and `-0.0` do not match.
slides.takeaway: Value 15, expected 10, CAS to 20: fails, value stays 15, `expected` becomes 15.

slides.title: Build any atomic update `x = f(x)`
items: Keep the body short and side-effect free.
`weak` may fail spuriously, so use it in a loop.
Lock-free, **not** wait-free: a thread can retry forever.

slides.lead: Only `std::atomic_flag` is guaranteed. Large types can hide a lock. Check `is_always_lock_free`.

slides.title: Pick by what must be protected
rows: A single RMW or a short CAS loop
Flag, counter, sequence number, pointer swap
Waiting threads should sleep, not burn CPU
slides.takeaway: An uncontended mutex stays in user space. A contended atomic bounces cache lines. Measure.

items.truth: `++`, `+=`, `fetch_*`, `exchange` and CAS are all atomic RMWs.
Memory order never affects atomicity. `relaxed` only drops ordering of other memory.

items.myth: "Atomic means the store buffer is flushed."
items.truth: Not a C++ guarantee. A relaxed store on x86 is a plain `mov`.
Identical on x86 (`lock cmpxchg`). Choose by whether you already loop.
It is lock-free: someone always succeeds, but one thread can starve.

items.myth: "Atomic always beats a mutex. A mutex always enters the kernel."
items.truth: Uncontended mutexes stay in user space. Contended atomics bounce cache lines.

slides.lead: Not a sequence. Not two variables. Save this, and follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
`counter` is a std::atomic<int>.
Two threads add 4 to it, 1000 times each. 🧵

What can it print? Comment your answer, then swipe ➜ to check it.
text.body: Two questions in one: the printed value, and whether this is a data race. Both parts matter.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: can you declare a `std::atomic<std::string>`? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. std::atomic<T> requires a trivially copyable T, and std::string is not, so it fails to compile. Protect the string with a mutex instead.

slides.title:
Expected 8000.
What can it print?

slides.verdict: C. No data race, but updates get lost
slides.verdict_sub: any multiple of 4 from 8 to 8000, run-dependent
bullets: `counter = counter + 4` is an atomic **load**, an add in a register, then an atomic **store**.
Both threads load 40, both store 44: one `+4` is lost.
Each half is atomic, so no UB. It is a race condition, not a data race.
Some runs print 8000. A passing run proves nothing.

slides.title: One operator changes everything
bullets: `x = x + 4` calls `operator int()` (a load), then `operator=` (a store).
Each half is atomic, so no sanitizer reports a data race. Only the result is wrong.
`+=`, `++` and `fetch_add` read and write in one indivisible step.
slides.takeaway: `x += 4` is one atomic RMW. `x = x + 4` is two atomic operations with a gap in between.

text.hook:
The single most asked detail about compare-and-swap.
What happens to `expected` when CAS fails? 🧠

Comment your answer, then swipe ➜ to check it.
text.body: Two CAS calls, two lines of output. Read the second call carefully.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: how do you atomically raise `std::atomic<int> m` to `v`, but only if `v` is larger? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: A CAS loop that re-checks every refreshed value: `int e = m.load(); while (e < v && !m.compare_exchange_weak(e, v)) {}`. `if (v > m.load()) m.store(v);` can lose the larger value.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: 15 != 10, so the first CAS fails and `value` stays 15.
On failure CAS **writes the current value** into `expected`: now 15.
The retry matches, `value` becomes 20. On success `expected` is untouched.

slides.title: Why CAS refreshes `expected`
bullets: A failed CAS hands you fresh data: no extra `load()`.
Recompute `desired` from it on every try.
`weak` in a loop, `strong` for one-shot decisions.
slides.takeaway: CAS failure: returns `false`, atomic unchanged, `expected` = current value.

text.hook:
Wrap any struct in std::atomic and it is lock-free, right?

x86-64, GCC. Three types, three booleans. 🧩
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This one decides whether your "lock-free" design really is.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: x86-64, GCC, and the CPU has `cmpxchg16b`. Is a 16-byte `std::atomic` lock-free? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: With GCC, `is_lock_free()` reports false: the operations go through `libatomic` (link `-latomic`), even though the CPU has `cmpxchg16b`.

slides.title:
x86-64, GCC.
What does it print?
slides.code:
struct Small { int a, b; };      // 8 bytes
struct Large { long a, b, c; };  // 24 bytes

using std::atomic;
std::cout << std::boolalpha
  << atomic<int*>::is_always_lock_free << ' '
  << atomic<Small>::is_always_lock_free << ' '
  << atomic<Large>::is_always_lock_free;

bullets: Pointers and 8-byte trivially copyable structs fit one native atomic instruction.
24 bytes do not: GCC uses a lock inside `libatomic` (link with `-latomic`).
Still fully atomic. Just not lock-free.
Platform-specific: only `std::atomic_flag` is guaranteed lock-free.

slides.title: Do not assume. Assert.
bullets: `a.is_lock_free()`: runtime, per object.
`std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free`: `constexpr`, C++17.
`ATOMIC_INT_LOCK_FREE` etc.: 0 never, 1 sometimes, 2 always.
slides.takeaway: A "lock-free" algorithm built on `std::atomic<Large>` silently contains a lock.

text.hook:
"It's just a bool stop flag. The CPU writes a bool atomically."

Does it still need std::atomic<bool>? 🧠
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: The code is 5 lines. What the optimizer does with it surprises a lot of people.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up: the flag publishes no other data. Which memory order is enough for its load and store? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: `memory_order_relaxed`. It is still fully atomic; release/acquire is only needed when the flag publishes other data.

slides.title: Does this flag need `std::atomic`?
options: No. A bool write is atomic on every CPU.
Yes. It is a data race (UB).
No. It stops within an iteration or two.

slides.verdict_sub: Plain concurrent read + write is a data race: undefined behaviour
bullets: Same location, two threads, one writes, not atomic, no sync: **data race**.
GCC `-O2`: reads `running` once, then loops forever. At `-O0` it stops.
`std::atomic<bool>` forces a real load on every iteration.
slides.cta: Why not A, C or D ➜

items: A: hardware atomicity is not C++ synchronization. The optimizer reasons with the language rules.
C: there is no such guarantee. The loop may never re-read the flag.
D: `volatile` forces re-reads in practice, but it is still a data race with no ordering.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "any variable written by one thread and read by another needs an atomic or a lock, even a bool."

text.hook:
One std::atomic<long> counter, shared by every thread.
Add more threads and it gets slower, not faster. Why? 🧠

Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: No mutex, no lock, and it still does not scale. The reason lives below the C++ level.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: on x86-64 (GCC -O2), `x.fetch_add(1)` is one `lock xadd`. What does `x.fetch_or(m)` compile to when its result is used? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: A `lock cmpxchg` retry loop. x86 has no single instruction that ORs and returns the old value, so this fetch_or is not wait-free there.

slides.title: Many threads call `hits.fetch_add(1)` on one `std::atomic<long>`. Why does it not scale?
options: `std::atomic<long>` takes a hidden lock on every `fetch_add`.
Every `fetch_add` needs exclusive ownership of one cache line, which ping-pongs between cores.

slides.verdict_sub: Contention lives at the cache-line level
bullets: Every RMW needs the line in exclusive state: other copies are invalidated.
Operations serialize on line transfers. Throughput can drop as threads are added.
Fix: per-thread slots on separate lines, summed on read.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or C ➜

items: A: `atomic<long>` is lock-free on x86-64 (`lock xadd`). The cost is the cache line, not a lock.
B: false sharing is *independent* hot data in one line. Here all threads share one variable.
C: `fetch_add` is one locked instruction. It never enters the kernel.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "scale writes by not sharing them. Pad per-thread state to separate cache lines."
